title: Synthetic genome shuffling of poxviruses in yeast generates novel poxvirus candidates with potential oncolytic properties
abstract: Oncolytic viruses represent a promising class of biotherapeutics, yet their clinical performance is often constrained by limited cytolytic potency and insufficient immune activation. To address these limitations, we developed a synthetic biology framework that applies genome-scale recombination in yeast to generate chimeric poxviruses derived from multiple non-human-pathogenic poxvirus lineages. We first established the near-complete assembly of a vaccinia virus genome within yeast and demonstrated its ability to yield a functional virus in human cancer cells, providing a modular foundation for genome engineering. Building on this platform, we combined genomic inputs from different poxvirus species to create a diverse library of chimeric constructs, a subset of which could be recovered as infectious particles. Phenotypic characterization revealed substantial variation among chimeras, including distinct plaque morphologies, spreading behaviors, and activity across human cancer cell lines, indicating the emergence of functional diversity rather than incremental modification. Whole-genome sequencing confirmed that individual chimeras integrated genetic segments from several parental species, validating the broad recombination capacity of the yeast-based system. Collectively, these results establish a conceptual advance in synthetic virology. Yeast-mediated genome shuffling enables the rapid generation of functionally diverse chimeric poxviruses from multispecies inputs, providing a flexible and scalable platform for the identification and development of future oncolytic poxvirus candidates. While the chimeric viruses described here do not yet contain the attenuating mutations required for tumor-selective replication, they provide a foundation for the engineering of next-generation oncolytic biotherapeutics.

title: LABORATORY-SCALE CULTIVATION OF THE OSPA-VAKTSINA VACCINIA VIRUS STRAIN IN VERO CELLS ON BIONOC II® MACROCARRIERS USING THE BELLOSTAGETM-3000 SYSTEM
abstract: Vaccinia virus remains relevant as a viral substrate for smallpox vaccines and as an orthopoxvirus model. This study evaluated, at laboratory scale, the feasibility of cultivating the “Ospa-vaktsina” vaccinia virus strain in Vero cells grown on BioNOC II® macrocarriers using the BelloStageTM-3000 Tide Motion system. The study was not designed as a comparative assessment of BelloStageTM-3000 performance against another cultivation platform. Vero cells were cultivated in BelloCell®-500A vessels in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium supplemented with 2% fetal bovine serum. After 120 h of cell cultivation, when the total cell number reached 1.99 × 109 cells per vessel, cultures were infected with a working virus inoculum at a calculated infectious input of 0.01 TCID50 per cell. The infectious input was calculated as the total TCID50 delivered in the 500-mL inoculum divided by the total cell number at infection. One bioreactor run included three parallel BelloCell®-500A vessels (n = 3 culture units within a single run). Cell attachment to the macrocarriers was 89% at 3 h after seeding. The total cell number increased from 7.45 × 107 cells at seeding to 1.99 × 109 cells per vessel at 120 h, corresponding to a 26.7-fold increase. Following infection, the virus titer increased from 4.60 log10 TCID50/mL in the working inoculum to a maximum of 6.00 log10 TCID50/mL at 120 h post-infection, a 1.40-log10 (approximately 25.1-fold) increase. Culture medium parameters were maintained within predefined operating ranges for the cell-growth and post-infection phases. Under the conditions tested, the Vero/BioNOC II® culture supported replication of the “Ospa-vaktsina” strain in BelloStageTM-3000. Because the study comprised a single bioreactor run and did not include a parallel comparator platform, the findings demonstrate laboratory-scale feasibility but do not establish technological superiority, process scalability, or suitability for vaccine manufacturing.

title: EVALUATION OF THE BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY OF ORTHOPOXVIRUS STRAINS IN PRIMARY CHICKEN EMBRYO FIBROBLASTS
abstract: Understanding the biological features of the genus, Orthopoxvirus, including their replicative activity, is essential for their application in virology and vaccinology. Comparative analysis of biological activity in cell cultures makes it possible to evaluate the replicative potential of strains and the degree of their adaptation to the cellular substrate. The aim of the study was to standardize a method for obtaining primary chicken embryo fibroblasts (CEF) and to use them as an in vitro substrate for assessing the biological activity of various Orthopoxvirus strains, with an emphasis on cytopathic effect (CPE) and infectious activity. Vaccinia virus, cowpox virus, and camelpox virus were used in the study. Primary CEF were obtained from 9-11-day embryonated chicken eggs (ECE), the optimal seeding concentration for the formation of a monolayer substrate was determined, and the cultures were infected with the viruses under study; CPE and virus titer were assessed during sequential passages. The results showed that a seeding concentration of 5×105 cells/mL ensured the formation of a uniform CEF monolayer within 24 h. Upon infection, all three viruses induced similar CPE, characterized by cell rounding, loss of elongated morphology, and partial destruction of the monolayer, with the main difference being the timing of CPE onset. Vaccinia virus strains induced CPE within 24 h, whereas cowpox virus and camelpox virus induced CPE after 36 and 48 h, respectively. Both vaccinia virus strains exhibited high infectious activity and rapid adaptation (titers from 5.50 to 6.58±0.12 lg TCID50/mL), whereas cowpox and camelpox viruses showed a lower and stable titer (titers from 5.50 to 6.58±0.12 lg TCID50/mL), and delayed CPE development. The results emphasize the significance of CPE onset time and infectious titer level as key parameters for evaluating replicative capacity and strain adaptation, which is important for laboratory studies and the selection of vaccine candidates.

title: Airborne transmission risk of monkeypox virus: the importance of infection-competent virus.
abstract: Zhaoliang Chen and colleagues1 propose that quantitative PCR (qPCR) cycle threshold (Ct) values exceeding 35 in massive-volume air sampling should not be equated with airborne transmissibility for monkeypox virus. Although this opinion might have practical utility, it does not address the fundamental biological basis for estimating transmissibility: the material being detected must be infectious for there to be transmission potential. We argue that a Ct value alone should not be considered as evidence of transmission potential, as qPCR cannot distinguish between nucleic acid from infection-competent virions and nucleic acid from degraded virions that pose no infection potential and therefore no transmission potential.

elements_en.main_results: The study does not report any direct results or numerical findings but raises a critical point about the interpretation of qPCR Ct values in assessing airborne transmission potential.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that qPCR alone cannot determine transmission potential, as it cannot differentiate between infection-competent virions and degraded virions, and they emphasize the need for a more accurate biological basis for estimating transmissibility.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that current methods for assessing airborne transmission risk of monkeypox virus may be insufficient, which has implications for public health surveillance and risk assessment strategies.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a theoretical discussion and does not present empirical data, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment based on the lack of direct experimental evidence.

title_zh: 空气传播的猴痘病毒 传播 风险:具有感染能力的病毒的重要性。
source_body_en: Zhaoliang Chen and colleagues1 propose that quantitative PCR (qPCR) cycle threshold (Ct) values exceeding 35 in massive-volume air sampling should not be equated with airborne transmissibility for monkeypox virus. Although this opinion might have practical utility, it does not address the fundamental biological basis for estimating transmissibility: the material being detected must be infectious for there to be transmission potential. We argue that a Ct value alone should not be considered as evidence of transmission potential, as qPCR cannot distinguish between nucleic acid from infection-competent virions and nucleic acid from degraded virions that pose no infection potential and therefore no transmission potential.
abstract_zh: 陈兆良及其同事1提出,大量空气采样中定量PCR(qPCR)循环阈值(Ct)超过35不应等同于猴痘病毒的空气传播能力。尽管这种观点可能具有实际用途,但它并没有解决估计传播性的基本生物学基础:被检测的材料必须具有传染性,才有 传播 的潜力。我们认为,单独的 Ct 值不应被视为 传播 潜力的证据,因为 qPCR 无法区分来自具有感染能力的病毒体的核酸和来自不具有感染潜力的降解病毒体的核酸,因此不具有 传播 潜力。

title: Mpox (Formerly Known as Monkeypox) in Dermatological Practice: Presentation of a Series of Four Clinical Cases at a Referral Hospital

source_records.title: Mpox (Formerly Known as Monkeypox) in Dermatological Practice: Presentation of a Series of Four Clinical Cases at a Referral Hospital

full_text: AbstractMpox (formerly known as monkeypox) has re-emerged globally as a significant public health concern, with dermatology services occupying a key role in early recognition due to its predominant mucocutaneous manifestations. We present a series of four confirmed mpox cases diagnosed in April 2025 at a tertiary dermatology center in Jalisco, Mexico. All cases occurred in men who have sex with men, three of whom were living with HIV. Clinical presentations were heterogeneous, ranging from disseminated vesiculopustular eruptions with systemic symptoms to strictly localized, painful perianal lesions without prodrome. One case was initially misdiagnosed as herpes, underscoring the diagnostic complexity and potential overlap with other sexually transmitted dermatoses. Epidemiologic risk factors included recent unprotected sexual encounters and, in one case, recent travel. Diagnosis was confirmed by PCR and supported by compatible histopathology when performed. This cluster within a short timeframe reflects ongoing community transmission and highlights the importance of maintaining high clinical suspicion, integrating empathetic and stigma-free sexual history-taking, and leveraging epidemiologic clues for early detection. Increasing diagnostic awareness in dermatology practice is essential to mitigate under-recognition, guide timely management, and support containment strategies.Keywords: hiv aids, monkeypox, monkeypox diagnosis, monkeypox treatment, monkeypox virus DiscussionThis case series illustrates the evolving clinical spectrum of mpox and reinforces dermatology's critical role in early recognition and diagnosis. Since the 2022 global outbreak, mpox has demonstrated sustained transmission outside historically endemic regions, particularly among MSM [1,2]. Similar to international and national reports, the four cases in our series occurred exclusively in MSM, and three patients were living with HIV, a population shown to have higher incidence and occasionally more severe or atypical presentations [2,3,6]. Importantly, one patient in our series was immunocompetent, underscoring that mpox is not restricted to immunocompromised hosts. Compatible mucocutaneous manifestations may occur irrespective of HIV status, and epidemiologic exposure should therefore remain a central component of clinical suspicion [6].Classically, mpox presents with a systemic prodrome followed by disseminated vesiculopustular lesions [2]. However, consistent with recent literature, our findings highlight significant clinical heterogeneity: two patients presented with isolated, painful perianal lesions, whereas one experienced initial mucosal involvement with odynophagia preceding the development of cutaneous findings. These atypical presentations align with recent evidence describing localized anogenital disease and mucosal-first involvement in sexually acquired mpox, which can mimic other sexually transmitted infections such as herpes simplex virus infection or syphilis [2,3,6]. One of our cases was initially misdiagnosed as herpes, underscoring how mpox can masquerade as other dermatoses, potentially delaying appropriate management and containment measures.Herpes simplex infection, syphilis, and other sexually transmitted infections were therefore considered clinically relevant differential diagnoses in this series. Importantly, the diagnosis of mpox was not established solely through exclusion of these entities but was confirmed by PCR, with supportive histopathologic findings when performed. A uniform laboratory screening panel for every alternative sexually transmitted infection was not consistently documented in the available clinical records. Consequently, these infections are presented as clinically relevant differential diagnoses rather than as uniformly laboratory-excluded conditions.Epidemiologic information remains essential for diagnosis. All patients reported recent sexual exposure, consistent with reports identifying close and sexual contact networks as important drivers of transmission [2-4]. Prompt PCR confirmation and histopathologic assessment when performed supported the diagnostic process. The identification of four confirmed cases within a single month at our center suggests ongoing regional transmission and potential under-recognition, consistent with continued surveillance reports in Mexico and internationally [4,5].Vaccination represents an additional component of mpox prevention. Vaccines based on vaccinia virus, including Modified Vaccinia Ankara-Bavarian Nordic (MVA-BN) and LC16m8, are recommended by the World Health Organization for individuals at increased risk of exposure according to epidemiologic circumstances, individual risk, vaccine availability, and national public health policies [7]. Vaccine availability remains heterogeneous among countries. In the United States, JYNNEOS, an MVA-BN vaccine, is recommended for individuals at increased risk of mpox and may also be used for post-exposure prophylaxis when clinically indicated [8]. Although vaccination was not the focus of the present case series, awareness of available preventive strategies complements timely clinical recognition and public health containment.Our findings reinforce the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for mpox in patients presenting with vesiculopustular, mucosal, genital, or anogenital lesions, particularly when epidemiologic risk factors are present. Importantly, such suspicion should not depend exclusively on HIV status or the presence of systemic symptoms. A non-judgmental, detailed sexual history is indispensable for reducing missed diagnoses and stigma-related barriers to care [2,3]. Ongoing physician education and clear clinical protocols are necessary to ensure timely identification and mitigate further spread [2,4,6].Several limitations should be acknowledged. This report represents a small retrospective case series from a single tertiary referral center. CD4 counts, HIV viral loads, specific antiretroviral regimens, and complete tecovirimat dosing and duration data were not consistently available in the clinical records. Likewise, laboratory testing for alternative sexually transmitted infections was not uniformly documented. Consequently, the present series was not designed to assess associations between immunologic status, specific antiretroviral or antiviral therapies, and disease severity. Nevertheless, these limitations do not affect the confirmed diagnosis of mpox in the reported cases or the primary descriptive objective of illustrating its heterogeneous dermatologic presentations. ConclusionsThis case series highlights the diverse clinical spectrum of mpox encountered in dermatologic practice, ranging from classic disseminated vesiculopustular disease to localized anogenital presentations with limited or absent systemic manifestations. The predominance of MSM and individuals living with HIV in this series is consistent with reported epidemiologic patterns; however, the occurrence of disease in an immunocompetent patient emphasizes that clinical suspicion should not depend exclusively on immune status.Early diagnosis relies on recognizing atypical forms, maintaining a broad differential diagnosis, and integrating thorough, stigma-free sexual and travel history-taking into routine assessment. Strengthening clinician awareness, ensuring timely access to diagnostic testing, and promoting preventive strategies, including vaccination when indicated and available, are important for avoiding misdiagnosis, enabling prompt management, and supporting public health containment efforts. Continued surveillance and reporting remain essential to better characterize evolving transmission patterns and the clinical behavior of mpox in diverse populations. IntroductionMpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is an emerging zoonotic infection caused by an orthopoxvirus, which has transitioned from a sporadic, endemic disease in Central and West Africa to a global public health concern since 2022 [1,2]. Although transmission historically involved animal-human contact, recent outbreaks have demonstrated sustained human-to-human transmission, particularly through close physical and sexual contact, with a disproportionately high incidence among men who have sex with men (MSM) [2-4].The epidemiologic relevance of mpox has persisted beyond the initial 2022 multinational outbreak. According to World Health Organization surveillance, 63,692 laboratory-confirmed cases and 256 deaths were reported across 105 countries between January 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026 [5]. These data demonstrate continued global transmission and reinforce the importance of sustained clinical awareness even outside the initial outbreak period.Clinically, mpox is characterized by mucocutaneous lesions that classically progress from macules to vesicles and pustules; however, presentations are heterogeneous, and atypical forms confined to genital or perianal regions have been increasingly recognized [2,6]. Systemic manifestations such as fever, lymphadenopathy, and malaise may precede cutaneous findings but can be absent in a subset of patients, particularly those with localized disease [3]. Such variability may lead to diagnostic challenges and misclassification as other sexually associated dermatoses, including herpes simplex virus infection or syphilis, emphasizing the crucial role of dermatologists in timely recognition [2,3,6].In Mexico, rising mpox cases have been documented intermittently since the 2022 global outbreak, with surveillance demonstrating ongoing transmission [4]. Early identification remains essential to limit spread and initiate adequate supportive care. Given the evolving epidemiologic patterns and potential under-recognition, dermatology services must maintain a high index of suspicion and integrate thorough, stigma-free sexual and travel history-taking into routine practice.This report describes four confirmed mpox cases diagnosed over a one-month period in a tertiary referral center in Jalisco, Mexico, highlighting clinical heterogeneity and reinforcing the importance of epidemiologic context in dermatologic assessment and early diagnosis. Case presentationCase 1A 41-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV presented with a one-month history of a disseminated polymorphous eruption including pustules, umbilicated vesicles, and crusted lesions on the face, trunk, extremities, palms, soles, and oral mucosa. Systemic symptoms included pruritus, fever, and cervical/inguinal lymphadenopathy. He reported multiple male sexual partners and recent unprotected intercourse. The eruption was initially misdiagnosed as herpes simplex infection, delaying appropriate treatment. Skin biopsy was compatible with mpox (Figure 1).Figure 1(A) Dermatoscopy showing characteristic form for this lesion, (B) Distribution in the back (C) Lesions in the armTreatmentHe received symptomatic therapy with antipyretics, oral analgesics, antihistamines, and daily cleansing of lesions. Given his HIV status and extensive mucocutaneous involvement, tecovirimat was initiated.ResponseWithin the first week, systemic symptoms improved and lesions began to crust. By day 18 of treatment, nearly all lesions had fully resolved.Follow-UpAt four weeks, no new lesions were observed and all cutaneous and mucosal findings had healed without scarring or superinfection. His antiretroviral therapy was optimized after diagnosis.Case 2A 40-year-old man living with HIV (treatment interruption three months prior) presented with localized painful umbilicated papules forming perianal plaques. Symptoms began one week prior, following prodromal fatigue and diarrhea. He reported more than 100 male sexual partners and recent high-risk anal contact. Biopsy showed findings consistent with mpox (Figure 2).Figure 2Perianal lesionsTreatmentBecause of immunosuppression and severe perianal pain, he received nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), topical anesthetics, and hygiene measures. Tecovirimat was started due to clinical severity and uncontrolled HIV.ResponseHe experienced significant reduction in pain and inflammation within the first week. Lesions crusted and resolved completely by days 14 to 16.Follow-UpAt a three-week evaluation, all lesions had healed without functional impairment. He resumed antiretroviral therapy and was referred for sexual health counseling.Case 3A 28-year-old man without known comorbidities presented with fever, headache, asthenia, and diaphoresis, followed by oral and pharyngeal lesions causing odynophagia. Days later, non-painful genital and hand lesions developed. He reported sexual contact with men ~15 days before onset and recent travel to Guanajuato. Skin biopsy confirmed mpox (Figure 3).Figure 3(A) Dorsal penile cutaneous lesion (B) Perioral lesions (C) Lesion on the nasal alaTreatmentHe was managed with oral analgesics, hydration, and topical antiseptics. Due to severe odynophagia, topical lidocaine and short-course corticosteroids were used for symptom control. Antiviral therapy was not indicated as disease remained mild and he was immunocompetent.ResponseSystemic symptoms resolved within five days. Mucosal and cutaneous lesions crusted and detached over 10 to 14 days.Follow-UpAt a four-week visit, no recurrence or complications were present. Only mild post-inflammatory erythema persisted.Case 4A 32-year-old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy and a recent history of tuberculosis presented with localized painful umbilicated papules forming perianal plaques, without fever or prodromal symptoms. Symptoms began abruptly two days after unprotected sexual contact. PCR and biopsy were consistent with mpox (Figure 4).Figure 4(A and B) Perianal lesionsTreatmentHe received analgesics, daily cleansing, and topical lidocaine for pain. Because of his HIV status and history of opportunistic infection, tecovirimat was started early.ResponsePain improved markedly within 72 hours. Lesions showed rapid crusting and resolution during the following week, without bacterial superinfection.Follow-UpBy the three-week follow-up visit, lesions had completely resolved with no scarring. His HIV parameters remained stable under ongoing antiretroviral therapy. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractMpox (formerly known as monkeypox) has re-emerged globally as a significant public health concern, with dermatology services occupying a key role in early recognition due to its predominant mucocutaneous manifestations. We present a series of four confirmed mpox cases diagnosed in April 2025 at a tertiary dermatology center in Jalisco, Mexico. All cases occurred in men who have sex with men, three of whom were living with HIV. Clinical presentations were heterogeneous, ranging from disseminated vesiculopustular eruptions with systemic symptoms to strictly localized, painful perianal lesions without prodrome. One case was initially misdiagnosed as herpes, underscoring the diagnostic complexity and potential overlap with other sexually transmitted dermatoses. Epidemiologic risk factors included recent unprotected sexual encounters and, in one case, recent travel. Diagnosis was confirmed by PCR and supported by compatible histopathology when performed. This cluster within a short timeframe reflects ongoing community transmission and highlights the importance of maintaining high clinical suspicion, integrating empathetic and stigma-free sexual history-taking, and leveraging epidemiologic clues for early detection. Increasing diagnostic awareness in dermatology practice is essential to mitigate under-recognition, guide timely management, and support containment strategies.Keywords: hiv aids, monkeypox, monkeypox diagnosis, monkeypox treatment, monkeypox virus
full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis case series illustrates the evolving clinical spectrum of mpox and reinforces dermatology's critical role in early recognition and diagnosis. Since the 2022 global outbreak, mpox has demonstrated sustained transmission outside historically endemic regions, particularly among MSM [1,2]. Similar to international and national reports, the four cases in our series occurred exclusively in MSM, and three patients were living with HIV, a population shown to have higher incidence and occasionally more severe or atypical presentations [2,3,6]. Importantly, one patient in our series was immunocompetent, underscoring that mpox is not restricted to immunocompromised hosts. Compatible mucocutaneous manifestations may occur irrespective of HIV status, and epidemiologic exposure should therefore remain a central component of clinical suspicion [6].Classically, mpox presents with a systemic prodrome followed by disseminated vesiculopustular lesions [2]. However, consistent with recent literature, our findings highlight significant clinical heterogeneity: two patients presented with isolated, painful perianal lesions, whereas one experienced initial mucosal involvement with odynophagia preceding the development of cutaneous findings. These atypical presentations align with recent evidence describing localized anogenital disease and mucosal-first involvement in sexually acquired mpox, which can mimic other sexually transmitted infections such as herpes simplex virus infection or syphilis [2,3,6]. One of our cases was initially misdiagnosed as herpes, underscoring how mpox can masquerade as other dermatoses, potentially delaying appropriate management and containment measures.Herpes simplex infection, syphilis, and other sexually transmitted infections were therefore considered clinically relevant differential diagnoses in this series. Importantly, the diagnosis of mpox was not established solely through exclusion of these entities but was confirmed by PCR, with supportive histopathologic findings when performed. A uniform laboratory screening panel for every alternative sexually transmitted infection was not consistently documented in the available clinical records. Consequently, these infections are presented as clinically relevant differential diagnoses rather than as uniformly laboratory-excluded conditions.Epidemiologic information remains essential for diagnosis. All patients reported recent sexual exposure, consistent with reports identifying close and sexual contact networks as important drivers of transmission [2-4]. Prompt PCR confirmation and histopathologic assessment when performed supported the diagnostic process. The identification of four confirmed cases within a single month at our center suggests ongoing regional transmission and potential under-recognition, consistent with continued surveillance reports in Mexico and internationally [4,5].Vaccination represents an additional component of mpox prevention. Vaccines based on vaccinia virus, including Modified Vaccinia Ankara-Bavarian Nordic (MVA-BN) and LC16m8, are recommended by the World Health Organization for individuals at increased risk of exposure according to epidemiologic circumstances, individual risk, vaccine availability, and national public health policies [7]. Vaccine availability remains heterogeneous among countries. In the United States, JYNNEOS, an MVA-BN vaccine, is recommended for individuals at increased risk of mpox and may also be used for post-exposure prophylaxis when clinically indicated [8]. Although vaccination was not the focus of the present case series, awareness of available preventive strategies complements timely clinical recognition and public health containment.Our findings reinforce the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for mpox in patients presenting with vesiculopustular, mucosal, genital, or anogenital lesions, particularly when epidemiologic risk factors are present. Importantly, such suspicion should not depend exclusively on HIV status or the presence of systemic symptoms. A non-judgmental, detailed sexual history is indispensable for reducing missed diagnoses and stigma-related barriers to care [2,3]. Ongoing physician education and clear clinical protocols are necessary to ensure timely identification and mitigate further spread [2,4,6].Several limitations should be acknowledged. This report represents a small retrospective case series from a single tertiary referral center. CD4 counts, HIV viral loads, specific antiretroviral regimens, and complete tecovirimat dosing and duration data were not consistently available in the clinical records. Likewise, laboratory testing for alternative sexually transmitted infections was not uniformly documented. Consequently, the present series was not designed to assess associations between immunologic status, specific antiretroviral or antiviral therapies, and disease severity. Nevertheless, these limitations do not affect the confirmed diagnosis of mpox in the reported cases or the primary descriptive objective of illustrating its heterogeneous dermatologic presentations.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsThis case series highlights the diverse clinical spectrum of mpox encountered in dermatologic practice, ranging from classic disseminated vesiculopustular disease to localized anogenital presentations with limited or absent systemic manifestations. The predominance of MSM and individuals living with HIV in this series is consistent with reported epidemiologic patterns; however, the occurrence of disease in an immunocompetent patient emphasizes that clinical suspicion should not depend exclusively on immune status.Early diagnosis relies on recognizing atypical forms, maintaining a broad differential diagnosis, and integrating thorough, stigma-free sexual and travel history-taking into routine assessment. Strengthening clinician awareness, ensuring timely access to diagnostic testing, and promoting preventive strategies, including vaccination when indicated and available, are important for avoiding misdiagnosis, enabling prompt management, and supporting public health containment efforts. Continued surveillance and reporting remain essential to better characterize evolving transmission patterns and the clinical behavior of mpox in diverse populations.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionMpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is an emerging zoonotic infection caused by an orthopoxvirus, which has transitioned from a sporadic, endemic disease in Central and West Africa to a global public health concern since 2022 [1,2]. Although transmission historically involved animal-human contact, recent outbreaks have demonstrated sustained human-to-human transmission, particularly through close physical and sexual contact, with a disproportionately high incidence among men who have sex with men (MSM) [2-4].The epidemiologic relevance of mpox has persisted beyond the initial 2022 multinational outbreak. According to World Health Organization surveillance, 63,692 laboratory-confirmed cases and 256 deaths were reported across 105 countries between January 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026 [5]. These data demonstrate continued global transmission and reinforce the importance of sustained clinical awareness even outside the initial outbreak period.Clinically, mpox is characterized by mucocutaneous lesions that classically progress from macules to vesicles and pustules; however, presentations are heterogeneous, and atypical forms confined to genital or perianal regions have been increasingly recognized [2,6]. Systemic manifestations such as fever, lymphadenopathy, and malaise may precede cutaneous findings but can be absent in a subset of patients, particularly those with localized disease [3]. Such variability may lead to diagnostic challenges and misclassification as other sexually associated dermatoses, including herpes simplex virus infection or syphilis, emphasizing the crucial role of dermatologists in timely recognition [2,3,6].In Mexico, rising mpox cases have been documented intermittently since the 2022 global outbreak, with surveillance demonstrating ongoing transmission [4]. Early identification remains essential to limit spread and initiate adequate supportive care. Given the evolving epidemiologic patterns and potential under-recognition, dermatology services must maintain a high index of suspicion and integrate thorough, stigma-free sexual and travel history-taking into routine practice.This report describes four confirmed mpox cases diagnosed over a one-month period in a tertiary referral center in Jalisco, Mexico, highlighting clinical heterogeneity and reinforcing the importance of epidemiologic context in dermatologic assessment and early diagnosis. Case presentationCase 1A 41-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV presented with a one-month history of a disseminated polymorphous eruption including pustules, umbilicated vesicles, and crusted lesions on the face, trunk, extremities, palms, soles, and oral mucosa. Systemic symptoms included pruritus, fever, and cervical/inguinal lymphadenopathy. He reported multiple male sexual partners and recent unprotected intercourse. The eruption was initially misdiagnosed as herpes simplex infection, delaying appropriate treatment. Skin biopsy was compatible with mpox (Figure 1).Figure 1(A) Dermatoscopy showing characteristic form for this lesion, (B) Distribution in the back (C) Lesions in the armTreatmentHe received symptomatic therapy with antipyretics, oral analgesics, antihistamines, and daily cleansing of lesions. Given his HIV status and extensive mucocutaneous involvement, tecovirimat was initiated.ResponseWithin the first week, systemic symptoms improved and lesions began to crust. By day 18 of treatment, nearly all lesions had fully resolved.Follow-UpAt four weeks, no new lesions were observed and all cutaneous and mucosal findings had healed without scarring or superinfection. His antiretroviral therapy was optimized after diagnosis.Case 2A 40-year-old man living with HIV (treatment interruption three months prior) presented with localized painful umbilicated papules forming perianal plaques. Symptoms began one week prior, following prodromal fatigue and diarrhea. He reported more than 100 male sexual partners and recent high-risk anal contact. Biopsy showed findings consistent with mpox (Figure 2).Figure 2Perianal lesionsTreatmentBecause of immunosuppression and severe perianal pain, he received nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), topical anesthetics, and hygiene measures. Tecovirimat was started due to clinical severity and uncontrolled HIV.ResponseHe experienced significant reduction in pain and inflammation within the first week. Lesions crusted and resolved completely by days 14 to 16.Follow-UpAt a three-week evaluation, all lesions had healed without functional impairment. He resumed antiretroviral therapy and was referred for sexual health counseling.Case 3A 28-year-old man without known comorbidities presented with fever, headache, asthenia, and diaphoresis, followed by oral and pharyngeal lesions causing odynophagia. Days later, non-painful genital and hand lesions developed. He reported sexual contact with men ~15 days before onset and recent travel to Guanajuato. Skin biopsy confirmed mpox (Figure 3).Figure 3(A) Dorsal penile cutaneous lesion (B) Perioral lesions (C) Lesion on the nasal alaTreatmentHe was managed with oral analgesics, hydration, and topical antiseptics. Due to severe odynophagia, topical lidocaine and short-course corticosteroids were used for symptom control. Antiviral therapy was not indicated as disease remained mild and he was immunocompetent.ResponseSystemic symptoms resolved within five days. Mucosal and cutaneous lesions crusted and detached over 10 to 14 days.Follow-UpAt a four-week visit, no recurrence or complications were present. Only mild post-inflammatory erythema persisted.Case 4A 32-year-old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy and a recent history of tuberculosis presented with localized painful umbilicated papules forming perianal plaques, without fever or prodromal symptoms. Symptoms began abruptly two days after unprotected sexual contact. PCR and biopsy were consistent with mpox (Figure 4).Figure 4(A and B) Perianal lesionsTreatmentHe received analgesics, daily cleansing, and topical lidocaine for pain. Because of his HIV status and history of opportunistic infection, tecovirimat was started early.ResponsePain improved markedly within 72 hours. Lesions showed rapid crusting and resolution during the following week, without bacterial superinfection.Follow-UpBy the three-week follow-up visit, lesions had completely resolved with no scarring. His HIV parameters remained stable under ongoing antiretroviral therapy. All patients were men who have sex with men (MSM), with three living with HIV, reflecting the epidemiologic patterns observed in other regions.
analysis.methods: Diagnosis was confirmed by PCR and supported by compatible histopathology when performed. PCR and biopsy results were consistent with mpox, and the diagnostic process was aided by thorough sexual and travel history-taking.
analysis.main_results: All patients reported recent sexual exposure, with one patient having more than 100 male sexual partners and recent high-risk anal contact. analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the clinical presentations of mpox in dermatologic practice are diverse, ranging from classic disseminated disease to localized anogenital forms. analysis.summary_en: This study presents a case series of four confirmed mpox cases diagnosed at a tertiary dermatology center in Jalisco, Mexico, in April 2025. The cases highlight the evolving clinical spectrum of mpox, with presentations ranging from classic disseminated disease to localized anogenital forms. All patients were men who have sex with men (MSM), and three were living with HIV, consistent with global epidemiologic trends. Diagnosis was confirmed by PCR and supported by histopathology. The study underscores the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for mpox in patients with vesiculopustular or mucosal lesions, particularly when risk factors such as recent sexual exposure are present. However, the small sample size and single-center design limit the generalizability of the findings, resulting in moderate confidence in the observed patterns.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是对 2025 年 4 月至 2025 年 5 月期间在墨西哥哈利斯科州一家三级皮肤科中心诊断的四例 猴痘 确诊病例的回顾性病例系列。所有患者均为男男性行为者 (MSM),其中 3 例感染艾滋病毒,反映了在其他地区观察到的流行病学模式。
elements_zh.methods: 诊断 通过 PCR 得到证实,并在执行时得到兼容的组织病理学支持。PCR 和活检结果与 猴痘 一致,并且彻底的性行为史和旅行史记录有助于诊断过程。
elements_zh.main_results: 所有患者均报告近期有过性接触,其中一名患者有超过 100 名男性性伴侣且近期存在高风险肛门接触。这些病例表现出临床异质性,包括孤立的肛周病变和粘膜受累并伴有吞咽痛先于皮肤表现。活检显示结果与 猴痘 一致。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,猴痘 在皮肤病学实践中的临床表现多种多样,从经典的播散性疾病到局部肛门生殖器形式。这凸显了广泛区分 诊断 的必要性以及流行病学背景在早期检测中的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调了对水疱脓疱、粘膜、生殖器或肛门生殖器病变患者保持高度怀疑 猴痘 的重要性,特别是当存在流行病学危险因素时。他们还支持需要继续使用 监测 来更好地了解 传播 模式和临床行为。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于来自单个三级转诊中心的少量病例,这可能会影响普遍性。然而,确诊的诊断和一致的临床表现为观察到的模式提供了适度的证据。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在强调 猴痘 不断变化的临床谱,并强化皮肤科在早期识别和 诊断 中的作用。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是对 2025 年 4 月至 2025 年 5 月期间在墨西哥哈利斯科州一家三级皮肤科中心诊断的四例 猴痘 确诊病例的回顾性病例系列。所有患者均为男男性行为者 (MSM),其中 3 例感染艾滋病毒,反映了在其他地区观察到的流行病学模式。
analysis_zh.methods: 诊断 通过 PCR 得到证实,并在执行时得到兼容的组织病理学支持。PCR 和活检结果与 猴痘 一致,并且彻底的性行为史和旅行史记录有助于诊断过程。
analysis_zh.main_results: 所有患者均报告近期有过性接触,其中一名患者有超过 100 名男性性伴侣且近期存在高风险肛门接触。这些病例表现出临床异质性,包括孤立的肛周病变和粘膜受累并伴有吞咽痛先于皮肤表现。活检显示结果与 猴痘 一致。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,猴痘 在皮肤病学实践中的临床表现多种多样,从经典的播散性疾病到局部肛门生殖器形式。这凸显了广泛区分 诊断 的必要性以及流行病学背景在早期检测中的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调了对水疱脓疱、粘膜、生殖器或肛门生殖器病变患者保持高度怀疑 猴痘 的重要性,特别是当存在流行病学危险因素时。他们还支持需要继续使用 监测 来更好地了解 传播 模式和临床行为。

title: AIRIME: a scalable adaptive RIME algorithm for feature optimization and data-driven monkeypox disease prediction
abstract: The rapid growth of big data in recent applications has created a pressing need for scalable and efficient optimization algorithms capable of handling large-scale and high-dimensional problems. Addressing this challenge, an Adaptive Improved Rime-Ice Optimization algorithm (AIRIME) is proposed which is built on the physics-based RIME algorithm inspired by the formation of soft and hard rime on surfaces. While RIME offers a strong theoretical foundation, it is hindered by limited exploratory capability, slow convergence, and an imbalance between exploration and exploitation. AIRIME introduces four key enhancements, including Adaptive k-Average-Best Mutation (AKAB), Adaptive Searching Process (ASP), Enhanced Solution Quality (ESQ), and Gaussian-Based Optimal Solution Mutation (GBOM), to overcome these challenges and meet the requirements of big data applications. AIRIME was rigorously tested on 41 functions from the CEC2017 and CEC2022 test suites, outperforming various classical, recent and advanced algorithms. Statistical evaluations, including Friedman rank and Wilcoxon rank tests, validated its superior performance and robustness. Sensitivity analyses further demonstrated the adaptability and efficiency of the proposed strategies. Moreover, a binary version of AIRIME was applied to feature selection (FS) tasks across 14 datasets, achieving promising results compared to various established binary metaheuristics. Furthermore, its real-world applicability was demonstrated in a novel Monkeypox disease prediction framework, where AIRIME helped to achieve an exceptional classification accuracy of 95.52% while selecting significantly fewer features, underscoring its efficiency in classifying high-dimensional healthcare data. Thus, AIRIME represents a significant advancement in big data-driven optimization, combining scalability, adaptability, and robustness to address complex and high-dimensional challenges across various domains, including critical healthcare applications.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the need for scalable and efficient optimization algorithms to handle large-scale and high-dimensional problems, particularly in the context of big data applications. The background highlights the growing importance of such algorithms in managing complex data sets.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the development and testing of the AIRIME algorithm on 41 benchmark functions from the CEC2017 and CEC2022 test suites, as well as its application to 14 datasets for feature selection tasks. The algorithm was also evaluated for its real-world applicability in a monkeypox disease prediction framework.
analysis.methods: The AIRIME algorithm was enhanced with four key strategies: Adaptive k-Average-Best Mutation (AKAB), Adaptive Searching Process (ASP), Enhanced Solution Quality (ESQ), and Gaussian-Based Optimal Solution Mutation (GBOM). These were implemented to improve the algorithm's performance in handling high-dimensional data and to validate its effectiveness through statistical tests such as Friedman rank and Wilcoxon rank tests.
analysis.main_results: AIRIME outperformed various classical, recent, and advanced algorithms on the CEC2017 and CEC2022 test suites. Sensitivity analyses confirmed its adaptability and efficiency, and its binary version achieved promising results in feature selection tasks. Additionally, it demonstrated exceptional classification accuracy of 95.52% in a monkeypox disease prediction framework while selecting significantly fewer features.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret these results as evidence of AIRIME's significant advancement in big data-driven optimization, particularly in its ability to address complex and high-dimensional challenges in healthcare applications. The novelty lies in its adaptability, scalability, and robustness for real-world use.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that AIRIME can be used to improve the accuracy and efficiency of disease prediction frameworks, particularly for monkeypox, by optimizing feature selection in high-dimensional healthcare data. This has implications for better surveillance and early detection systems.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to benchmark functions and datasets, which may not fully represent real-world complexities. However, the results are supported by rigorous statistical evaluations, indicating a moderate level of confidence in the algorithm's performance.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces the AIRIME algorithm, an Adaptive Improved Rime-Ice Optimization algorithm designed to address the challenges of handling large-scale and high-dimensional data in big data applications. The algorithm was tested on 41 benchmark functions from the CEC2017 and CEC2022 test suites, outperforming various classical, recent, and advanced algorithms. Additionally, its binary version was applied to 14 datasets for feature selection tasks, achieving promising results. The algorithm was also demonstrated in a monkeypox disease prediction framework, where it achieved an exceptional classification accuracy of 95.52% while selecting significantly fewer features. The authors interpret these results as a significant advancement in big data-driven optimization, particularly for healthcare applications. The study's findings suggest that AIRIME can improve disease prediction systems, especially for monkeypox, by optimizing feature selection in high-dimensional data. However, the study is limited to benchmark functions and datasets, which may not fully capture real-world complexities, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在解决对可扩展且高效的优化算法的需求,以处理大规模和高维问题,特别是在大数据应用的背景下。这一背景凸显了此类算法在管理复杂数据集方面日益重要。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及在 CEC2017 和 CEC2022 测试套件中的 41 个基准函数上开发和测试 AIRIME 算法,以及将其应用于 14 个数据集以执行特征选择任务。该算法还评估了其在猴痘疾病预测框架中的实际适用性。
elements_zh.methods: AIRIME 算法通过四个关键策略进行了增强:自适应 k 平均最佳 突变 (AKAB)、自适应搜索过程 (ASP)、增强解质量 (ESQ) 和基于高斯的最优解 突变 (GBOM)。实施这些措施是为了提高算法处理高维数据的性能,并通过弗里德曼等级和威尔科克森等级测试等统计测试来验证其有效性。
elements_zh.main_results: AIRIME 在 CEC2017 和 CEC2022 测试套件上的表现优于各种经典、最新和高级算法。敏感性分析证实了其适应性和效率,其二进制版本在特征选择任务中取得了可喜的结果。此外,它在猴痘疾病预测框架中表现出 95.52% 的出色分类准确率,同时选择的特征明显更少。

elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于基准函数和数据集,可能无法完全代表现实世界的复杂性。然而,这些结果得到了严格的统计评估的支持,表明对该算法的性能有一定的信心。

title_zh: AIRIME:一种可扩展的自适应 RIME 算法,用于特征优化和数据驱动的猴痘疾病预测
source_body_en: The rapid growth of big data in recent applications has created a pressing need for scalable and efficient optimization algorithms capable of handling large-scale and high-dimensional problems. Addressing this challenge, an Adaptive Improved Rime-Ice Optimization algorithm (AIRIME) is proposed which is built on the physics-based RIME algorithm inspired by the formation of soft and hard rime on surfaces. While RIME offers a strong theoretical foundation, it is hindered by limited exploratory capability, slow convergence, and an imbalance between exploration and exploitation. AIRIME introduces four key enhancements, including Adaptive k-Average-Best Mutation (AKAB), Adaptive Searching Process (ASP), Enhanced Solution Quality (ESQ), and Gaussian-Based Optimal Solution Mutation (GBOM), to overcome these challenges and meet the requirements of big data applications. AIRIME was rigorously tested on 41 functions from the CEC2017 and CEC2022 test suites, outperforming various classical, recent and advanced algorithms. Statistical evaluations, including Friedman rank and Wilcoxon rank tests, validated its superior performance and robustness. Sensitivity analyses further demonstrated the adaptability and efficiency of the proposed strategies. Moreover, a binary version of AIRIME was applied to feature selection (FS) tasks across 14 datasets, achieving promising results compared to various established binary metaheuristics. Furthermore, its real-world applicability was demonstrated in a novel Monkeypox disease prediction framework, where AIRIME helped to achieve an exceptional classification accuracy of 95.52% while selecting significantly fewer features, underscoring its efficiency in classifying high-dimensional healthcare data. Thus, AIRIME represents a significant advancement in big data-driven optimization, combining scalability, adaptability, and robustness to address complex and high-dimensional challenges across various domains, including critical healthcare applications.
abstract_zh: 最近应用中大数据的快速增长迫切需要能够处理大规模和高维问题的可扩展且高效的优化算法。为了解决这一挑战,提出了一种自适应改进雾凇-冰优化算法(AIRIME),该算法建立在基于物理的 RIME 算法的基础上,该算法受到表面软雾和硬雾凇形成的启发。虽然 RIME 提供了坚实的理论基础,但它受到有限的探索能力、缓慢的收敛以及探索与开发之间的不平衡的阻碍。AIRIME引入了四项关键增强功能,包括自适应k平均最佳突变(AKAB)、自适应搜索过程(ASP)、增强解质量(ESQ)和基于高斯的最优解突变(GBOM),以克服这些挑战并满足大数据应用的要求。AIRIME 在 CEC2017 和 CEC2022 测试套件的 41 项功能上进行了严格测试,性能优于各种经典、最新和高级算法。统计评估,包括 Friedman 等级和 Wilcoxon 等级检验,验证了其卓越的性能和稳健性。敏感性分析进一步证明了所提出策略的适应性和效率。此外,AIRIME 的二进制版本应用于 14 个数据集的特征选择 (FS) 任务,与各种已建立的二进制元启发法相比,取得了有希望的结果。此外,其在现实世界中的适用性在新型猴痘疾病预测框架中得到了证明,其中 AIRIME 帮助实现了 95.52% 的出色分类准确率,同时选择的特征明显减少,强调了其对高维医疗数据进行分类的效率。因此,AIRIME 代表了大数据驱动优化方面的重大进步,它将可扩展性、适应性和鲁棒性结合起来,以解决包括关键医疗保健应用在内的各个领域的复杂和高维挑战。

title: Disciform Keratitis That Improves With Poly(Adenosine Diphosphate-Ribose) Polymerase Inhibitor Treatment for Ovarian Cancer but Recurs Upon Discontinuation of Treatment

source_records.title: Disciform Keratitis That Improves With Poly(Adenosine Diphosphate-Ribose) Polymerase Inhibitor Treatment for Ovarian Cancer but Recurs Upon Discontinuation of Treatment

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: The patient was a 73-year-old woman. She underwent surgery for ovarian cancer but needed chemotherapy because tumor cells were observed at the resection margin. She was administered niraparib tosilate hydrate, a poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor, for five years; however, she developed severe malaise that made daily life difficult, rendering continued treatment impossible. Consequently, the PARP inhibitor was discontinued, and her physical condition improved. One year after discontinuation, she developed ocular herpes zoster, followed by disciform keratitis, leading to her presentation at our hospital. Examination of the right eye revealed disciform corneal edema and opacity, resulting in a diagnosis of disciform keratitis. Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA was detected via PCR analysis of the aqueous humor; treatment with oral valacyclovir and topical betamethasone was initiated. Subsequently, the disciform keratitis resolved with continued topical betamethasone therapy. However, ovarian cancer recurrence was observed, and another PARP inhibitor, olaparib, was prescribed. She again experienced malaise, necessitating the discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor. One month after discontinuation, a recurrence of disciform keratitis was observed. Frequent topical betamethasone administration was initiated, resulting in the resolution of the disciform keratitis. These findings suggest the possibility that in patients with cancer who are immunocompromised due to treatment with PARP inhibitors, an immune response against VZV does not occur; however, when immune function recovers upon discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor, the immune response against VZV is reactivated, resulting in the recurrence of disciform keratitis. Thus, when managing patients with cancer, it is essential to monitor fluctuations in immune response while addressing ocular infections and inflammatory diseases. DiscussionWhile herpetic keratitis is an ophthalmic disease, research in recent years has advanced beyond its purely ophthalmological aspects, such as diagnosis and treatment, to explore the relationship between the condition and systemic diseases. It has been reported that patients with diabetes face an increased risk of developing herpetic keratitis, as hyperglycemia can cause damage to the corneal epithelium [8]. In addition to the initial infection, the immune response plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis [5]. Patients infected with the HIV, a prototypical immunodeficiency condition, are reported to experience a higher incidence of severe herpetic keratitis and a greater likelihood of recurrence [9-11]. Diabetes has been shown not only to cause corneal epithelial damage but also to impair immune responses systemically [12]. Consequently, a compromised immune response is considered a potential factor contributing to the development of herpetic keratitis in diabetic patients. These findings reinforce the understanding that the immune response is critical to the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis [5].There have been reports of patients developing herpes simplex virus (HSV)-associated endotheliitis while receiving topical interferon (IFN)-α2b therapy for ocular surface squamous cell carcinoma [13]. Cases of disciform keratitis have also been reported in association with monkeypox virus (MPXV) infection, a condition frequently observed in immunocompromised individuals [14]. Although the condition initially resolved under the suspicion of herpetic keratitis, MPXV DNA was subsequently identified as the causative agent via PCR analysis of aqueous humor [14]. Thus, disciform keratitis can develop in various situations where immune suppression may occur. Furthermore, it is important to consider that pathogens not previously suspected of triggering disciform keratitis may also be potential causes of the condition.We encountered a case involving a patient with a history of ovarian cancer undergoing chemotherapy, in whom disciform keratitis developed, went into remission, and subsequently relapsed. The disciform keratitis resolved during treatment with a PARP inhibitor, a period characterized by systemic immunosuppression, but relapsed upon discontinuation of treatment. This pattern was observed repeatedly. As previously discussed, it is readily conceivable that the systemic immune response plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis, particularly in the development of disciform keratitis, which is driven by immune-mediated mechanisms. However, there have been no reports in clinical practice that compare and analyze fluctuations in a patient's immune status alongside the clinical course of disciform keratitis. The information obtained from this case may provide evidence that systemic immune status contributes to the recurrence of disciform keratitis. However, data on hematological and immunological parameters (such as CBC with leukocyte differential and lymphocyte counts) were not available. Furthermore, this report demonstrated an association in a single case; it does not establish a causal relationship. The assertion that systemic immune status influences the resolution or recurrence of lesions lacks support from actual immunological data, and therefore, the hypothesis has not been empirically verified and has limitations.Taken altogether, for patients with cancer, it is essential, not only for disciform keratitis but also for determining treatment strategies for any ophthalmic condition, to verify and fully understand the details of their ongoing medical treatment and to correlate these with clinical ocular findings. ConclusionsIn a patient with a history of ovarian cancer, disciform keratitis resolved during treatment with PARP inhibitors. However, the condition was observed to recur following the discontinuation of chemotherapy. It has been reported that the systemic immune response plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis, particularly in disciform keratitis, which is driven by immune-mediated mechanisms. There have been no previous reports in clinical practice comparing and examining the relationship between changes in a patient's immune status and the course of disciform keratitis; thus, the information obtained from this case may provide valuable, direct evidence that systemic immune status influences the clinical course of disciform keratitis. IntroductionA condition in which the cornea becomes swollen in a disc-shaped pattern and cloudy is called disciform keratitis. Initially, disciform keratitis was known as "Arlt's abscessus siccus." In 1901, Fuchs renamed the condition "disciform keratitis" [1]. Disciform keratitis causes visual impairment due to corneal edema, opacity, and anterior chamber inflammation; furthermore, it can lead to a loss of corneal endothelial cells and result in bullous keratopathy [2]. Although the etiology of disciform keratitis was initially unclear, reports subsequently identified herpesviruses as a primary cause [3]. Regarding the pathogenesis, as the concept of immunology gained academic recognition, it was demonstrated that the condition involves not merely viral infection but also the host's biological response, specifically an immune response to viral antigens, which plays a crucial role [4]. It is now understood that the pathophysiology of disciform keratitis involves corneal stromal infiltration (predominantly by mononuclear leukocytes such as lymphocytes) and keratic precipitates, accompanied by disciform stromal edema and microcystic edema localized to the affected area [5]. Since these inflammatory cells infiltrate the eye locally via the systemic circulation, systemic immune status may significantly influence the onset of disciform keratitis. Recent reports indicate that, in addition to herpesviruses, other pathogens such as Acanthamoeba [6] and microsporidia [7] can also induce disciform keratitis.As noted above, while disciform keratitis may be triggered by an infectious process, the immune response plays a primary role in the development of the clinical presentation. While immunosuppression typically exacerbates rather than cures viral infections, it can serve to suppress inflammation in cases where the immune response to viral antigens triggers an inflammatory reaction. This report discusses a case in a patient with cancer in which the administration of anticancer drugs influenced the resolution and recurrence of disciform keratitis. Case presentationThe patient was a 73-year-old woman. She underwent surgery for ovarian cancer but continued chemotherapy because tumor cells were observed at the resection margin. She was treated with the anticancer drug niraparib tosilate hydrate, a poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor, for five years; however, she developed severe malaise that made daily activities difficult (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE): grade 3), rendering continued treatment impossible. Consequently, the PARP inhibitor, which had been administered for five years, was discontinued, and her physical condition improved. One year after discontinuation, she noticed blurred vision with ocular pain and hyperemia. A few days later, she was diagnosed with ocular herpes zoster, followed by disciform keratitis, leading her to visit our hospital. At the initial examination, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 1.2 in both eyes, and intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg in the right eye and 11 mmHg in the left eye. Disciform corneal edema and opacity, together with keratic precipitates and anterior chamber cells, were observed in the right eye (Figure 1), and a diagnosis of disciform keratitis was made.Figure 1Slit-lamp photographs at the initial visit.(a) Low magnification; (b) high magnification. Disciform keratitis is observed in the central cornea (dotted circle).Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA was detected via PCR analysis of the aqueous humor; the patient was treated with oral valacyclovir for seven days and topical betamethasone, resulting in improvement.Table 1PCR results of aqueous humor samples.Type of pathogenPCR resultHerpes simplex virus type 1NegativeVaricella-zoster virusPositiveHerpes simplex virus type 2NegativeHuman herpesvirus 6NegativeEpstein-Barr virusNegativeCytomegalovirusNegativeHuman T-cell leukemia virus type 1NegativeTreponema pallidumNegativeToxoplasma gondiiNegativeSubsequently, the disciform keratitis resolved with continued topical betamethasone therapy (Figure 2).Figure 2Slit-lamp photograph two months after the initial visit.Disciform keratitis had resolved.Topical betamethasone therapy was completed six months after it began. Following a recurrence of ovarian cancer, the patient was prescribed olaparib, a PARP inhibitor. However, the patient again experienced physical deterioration (CTCAE: grade 3), leading to the discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor. One month after discontinuation, a recurrence of disciform keratitis was observed using the retroillumination method (Figure 3) because the lesion was mild.Figure 3Slit-lamp photograph one month after discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor olaparib.Retroillumination image. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionWhile herpetic keratitis is an ophthalmic disease, research in recent years has advanced beyond its purely ophthalmological aspects, such as diagnosis and treatment, to explore the relationship between the condition and systemic diseases. It has been reported that patients with diabetes face an increased risk of developing herpetic keratitis, as hyperglycemia can cause damage to the corneal epithelium [8]. In addition to the initial infection, the immune response plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis [5]. Patients infected with the HIV, a prototypical immunodeficiency condition, are reported to experience a higher incidence of severe herpetic keratitis and a greater likelihood of recurrence [9-11]. Diabetes has been shown not only to cause corneal epithelial damage but also to impair immune responses systemically [12]. Consequently, a compromised immune response is considered a potential factor contributing to the development of herpetic keratitis in diabetic patients. These findings reinforce the understanding that the immune response is critical to the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis [5].There have been reports of patients developing herpes simplex virus (HSV)-associated endotheliitis while receiving topical interferon (IFN)-α2b therapy for ocular surface squamous cell carcinoma [13]. Cases of disciform keratitis have also been reported in association with monkeypox virus (MPXV) infection, a condition frequently observed in immunocompromised individuals [14]. Although the condition initially resolved under the suspicion of herpetic keratitis, MPXV DNA was subsequently identified as the causative agent via PCR analysis of aqueous humor [14]. Thus, disciform keratitis can develop in various situations where immune suppression may occur. Furthermore, it is important to consider that pathogens not previously suspected of triggering disciform keratitis may also be potential causes of the condition.We encountered a case involving a patient with a history of ovarian cancer undergoing chemotherapy, in whom disciform keratitis developed, went into remission, and subsequently relapsed. The disciform keratitis resolved during treatment with a PARP inhibitor, a period characterized by systemic immunosuppression, but relapsed upon discontinuation of treatment. This pattern was observed repeatedly. As previously discussed, it is readily conceivable that the systemic immune response plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis, particularly in the development of disciform keratitis, which is driven by immune-mediated mechanisms. However, there have been no reports in clinical practice that compare and analyze fluctuations in a patient's immune status alongside the clinical course of disciform keratitis. The information obtained from this case may provide evidence that systemic immune status contributes to the recurrence of disciform keratitis. However, data on hematological and immunological parameters (such as CBC with leukocyte differential and lymphocyte counts) were not available. Furthermore, this report demonstrated an association in a single case; it does not establish a causal relationship. The assertion that systemic immune status influences the resolution or recurrence of lesions lacks support from actual immunological data, and therefore, the hypothesis has not been empirically verified and has limitations.Taken altogether, for patients with cancer, it is essential, not only for disciform keratitis but also for determining treatment strategies for any ophthalmic condition, to verify and fully understand the details of their ongoing medical treatment and to correlate these with clinical ocular findings.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsIn a patient with a history of ovarian cancer, disciform keratitis resolved during treatment with PARP inhibitors. However, the condition was observed to recur following the discontinuation of chemotherapy. It has been reported that the systemic immune response plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of herpetic keratitis, particularly in disciform keratitis, which is driven by immune-mediated mechanisms. There have been no previous reports in clinical practice comparing and examining the relationship between changes in a patient's immune status and the course of disciform keratitis; thus, the information obtained from this case may provide valuable, direct evidence that systemic immune status influences the clinical course of disciform keratitis.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionA condition in which the cornea becomes swollen in a disc-shaped pattern and cloudy is called disciform keratitis. Initially, disciform keratitis was known as "Arlt's abscessus siccus." In 1901, Fuchs renamed the condition "disciform keratitis" [1]. Disciform keratitis causes visual impairment due to corneal edema, opacity, and anterior chamber inflammation; furthermore, it can lead to a loss of corneal endothelial cells and result in bullous keratopathy [2]. Although the etiology of disciform keratitis was initially unclear, reports subsequently identified herpesviruses as a primary cause [3]. Regarding the pathogenesis, as the concept of immunology gained academic recognition, it was demonstrated that the condition involves not merely viral infection but also the host's biological response, specifically an immune response to viral antigens, which plays a crucial role [4]. It is now understood that the pathophysiology of disciform keratitis involves corneal stromal infiltration (predominantly by mononuclear leukocytes such as lymphocytes) and keratic precipitates, accompanied by disciform stromal edema and microcystic edema localized to the affected area [5]. Since these inflammatory cells infiltrate the eye locally via the systemic circulation, systemic immune status may significantly influence the onset of disciform keratitis. Recent reports indicate that, in addition to herpesviruses, other pathogens such as Acanthamoeba [6] and microsporidia [7] can also induce disciform keratitis.As noted above, while disciform keratitis may be triggered by an infectious process, the immune response plays a primary role in the development of the clinical presentation. While immunosuppression typically exacerbates rather than cures viral infections, it can serve to suppress inflammation in cases where the immune response to viral antigens triggers an inflammatory reaction. This report discusses a case in a patient with cancer in which the administration of anticancer drugs influenced the resolution and recurrence of disciform keratitis. Case presentationThe patient was a 73-year-old woman. She underwent surgery for ovarian cancer but continued chemotherapy because tumor cells were observed at the resection margin. She was treated with the anticancer drug niraparib tosilate hydrate, a poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor, for five years; however, she developed severe malaise that made daily activities difficult (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE): grade 3), rendering continued treatment impossible. Consequently, the PARP inhibitor, which had been administered for five years, was discontinued, and her physical condition improved. One year after discontinuation, she noticed blurred vision with ocular pain and hyperemia. A few days later, she was diagnosed with ocular herpes zoster, followed by disciform keratitis, leading her to visit our hospital. At the initial examination, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 1.2 in both eyes, and intraocular pressure was 12 mmHg in the right eye and 11 mmHg in the left eye. Disciform corneal edema and opacity, together with keratic precipitates and anterior chamber cells, were observed in the right eye (Figure 1), and a diagnosis of disciform keratitis was made.Figure 1Slit-lamp photographs at the initial visit.(a) Low magnification; (b) high magnification. Disciform keratitis is observed in the central cornea (dotted circle).Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA was detected via PCR analysis of the aqueous humor; the patient was treated with oral valacyclovir for seven days and topical betamethasone, resulting in improvement.Table 1PCR results of aqueous humor samples.Type of pathogenPCR resultHerpes simplex virus type 1NegativeVaricella-zoster virusPositiveHerpes simplex virus type 2NegativeHuman herpesvirus 6NegativeEpstein-Barr virusNegativeCytomegalovirusNegativeHuman T-cell leukemia virus type 1NegativeTreponema pallidumNegativeToxoplasma gondiiNegativeSubsequently, the disciform keratitis resolved with continued topical betamethasone therapy (Figure 2).Figure 2Slit-lamp photograph two months after the initial visit.Disciform keratitis had resolved.Topical betamethasone therapy was completed six months after it began. Following a recurrence of ovarian cancer, the patient was prescribed olaparib, a PARP inhibitor. However, the patient again experienced physical deterioration (CTCAE: grade 3), leading to the discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor. One month after discontinuation, a recurrence of disciform keratitis was observed using the retroillumination method (Figure 3) because the lesion was mild.Figure 3Slit-lamp photograph one month after discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor olaparib.Retroillumination image. Recurrence of disciform keratitis is observed (dotted circle).PARP: Poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase.Consequently, frequent topical betamethasone administration was initiated; the disciform keratitis improved, and there has been no recurrence for three months (Figure 4).Figure 4Slit-lamp photograph two months after discontinuation of the PARP inhibitor olaparib.Retroillumination image. The disciform keratitis had resolved.PARP: Poly(adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase.BCVA in both eyes remained around 1.2 during the observation period.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the relationship between immune status and the clinical course of disciform keratitis, particularly in the context of systemic immunosuppression caused by cancer treatments.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This case report describes a single patient with a history of ovarian cancer who developed disciform keratitis following discontinuation of PARP inhibitor therapy, highlighting the clinical course and immune status changes in this individual.
analysis.methods: Disciform keratitis was diagnosed via slit-lamp examination, and VZV DNA was detected using PCR analysis of aqueous humor. The patient was treated with oral valacyclovir and topical betamethasone, with clinical improvement observed.
analysis.main_results: Disciform keratitis resolved during PARP inhibitor treatment, which induced systemic immunosuppression, but recurred one year after discontinuation. PCR analysis confirmed the presence of VZV DNA in the aqueous humor.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that immune suppression from PARP inhibitors may prevent reactivation of VZV, leading to resolution of disciform keratitis, while immune recovery upon treatment discontinuation may reactivate the virus, causing recurrence.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study highlights the importance of monitoring immune status in cancer patients to manage ocular complications like disciform keratitis, particularly those associated with viral reactivation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single case, and the association observed does not establish causality. The evidence is considered moderate due to the lack of comparative data and immunological verification.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes a patient with ovarian cancer who developed disciform keratitis following discontinuation of PARP inhibitor treatment. The condition resolved during treatment with the PARP inhibitor, which induced systemic immunosuppression, but recurred one year after treatment cessation. PCR analysis of aqueous humor confirmed the presence of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA, suggesting a link between immune status and the clinical course of disciform keratitis. The findings imply that immune suppression may prevent viral reactivation, while immune recovery could lead to recurrence. However, the study is limited to a single case and does not establish causality, resulting in moderate evidence strength. The report underscores the need to monitor immune status in cancer patients to manage ocular complications associated with viral reactivation.
